title: When to stop coaching an underperformer
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: Luca Foppoli takes on the question that popular coaching advice avoids, which is what a manager should do when the other person does not respond. His answer is that you stop, whether the problem is the coach or the coachee and whether the person cannot or will not change. He builds the case on opportunity cost, since time spent on an unresponsive low performer is time taken from the rest of the team, and on the paradox that a person who has doubled a poor output feels he deserves praise. He sets a trigger for stopping, which is that you have created the conditions for success and given feedback on several different topics without change, and he rebuts the objection that three chances is too harsh. He then explains how to withdraw coaching well, keeping the standard visible, documenting the gap and walking the person to the exit, while admitting he does not know how to keep that person engaged.
points: The core argument is economic: coaching an unresponsive person consumes the manager's time at the expense of a team whose performance then stalls.
Foppoli sets a concrete stopping rule, which is feedback on three different things after the conditions for success are in place, since repeated failure shows a pattern.
He admits that earlier he saw himself as the shepherd who brings every sheep home, and reframes that as arrogance because people choose whether to change.
Stopping coaching is not stopping management, because the manager must keep the standard visible, keep a factual paper trail and prepare for a performance improvement plan.
He is candid about an unresolved problem, how to keep a withdrawn employee engaged, and invites readers to answer in the comments.
quotes: You stop. You stop whether the problem is the coach or the coachee and whether the coachee can’t change or won’t change.

In the meanwhile, the opportunity cost compounds against you, because the time you spent on your low performer is time you did NOT spend on the rest of the team, whose performance has stalled, if not drifted altogether
single-point accountability, clear expectations, a safe environment, given feedback repeatedly and nothing changed.
If you try coaching a person on three different things, he has had the opportunity to show a different behavior and failed to do so, it is a patter and it is reason enough to stop.
Some people simply cannot change and so a fourth attempt would fail just the same. And the others CHOOSE whether to change. Not you. Them.
You need to create a paper trail to document the standard-vs-performance gap, because you’ll need it to justify the negative performance review and the performance improvement plan.
Withdrawing coaching is a necessity, but doing it well is hard.
